slides: Welcome back, and now the bar chart. It's one of the most common charts on the exam.
A bar chart shows the same data as before, the table, the points and the lines. This time we use bars.

slides.say: On the left are the lines from the last lesson. On the right we'll build bars from the same data.
Let's start with the vehicles sold. Instead of the line, each year gets a bar from the bottom up to the point.
Two thousand ten up to sixty, two thousand eleven up to eighty, two thousand twelve also eighty, and two thousand thirteen up to a hundred.
at: Two thousand ten up to sixty

slides.say: The key changes too. A white bar now means the vehicles sold.
Next, the private cars. Their bars would fall inside the same place, so we move them a bit to the right.
We do the same with the other two columns. Now the bars of each year stand next to each other.
So a bar's height is its value. Let's check one. Two thousand ten, privately owned, the grey bar.
It reaches forty. So forty thousand vehicles were privately owned.
That's the same forty as the point in the line graph, and the same as in the table. The same data, three pictures.
at: the same as in the table

slides.say: Sometimes a bar stands inside another bar.
Here, the white bar is all the vehicles sold. In two thousand ten, it reaches sixty.
Inside it stands a black bar, the private cars. It reaches forty-five.
at: Inside it stands a black bar

slides.say: Why inside? Because the private cars are a part of the vehicles sold. Forty-five of the sixty.
A bar inside a bar can also hide an overlap question. Look at two thousand eleven.
Eighty thousand vehicles were sold. Of them, sixty thousand were private cars, and fifty thousand were privately owned.
How many were both, private cars and privately owned? It could be that all fifty are inside the sixty.
at: all fifty are inside the sixty

slides.say: Then all fifty are both.
Or we can push the fifty up, as high as it goes, to the top of the eighty.
Now only part of it is inside the sixty. How much? Sixty plus fifty is a hundred ten.
But there are only eighty vehicles. A hundred ten minus eighty is thirty. So at least thirty are both.
So both can be anywhere from thirty to fifty thousand. It's the same as in overlap questions.
Now another kind of bar chart. Here there are three kinds of vehicles. Private cars, commercial vehicles, and motorcycles.
A vehicle can be only one of them. It's a van or a car, not both.
at: A vehicle can be only one

slides.say: So we can put the bars one on top of the other. That's called stacked bars.
at: one on top of the other

slides: Why would we want that? Say I own the dealer group. Most of all, I want the total.

slides.say: The top of the stack is the total. In two thousand twelve it's almost a hundred twenty. About a hundred eighteen thousand.
at: The top of the stack is the total

slides.say: And how many commercial vehicles were sold in two thousand twelve? The grey part goes from sixty up to a hundred ten.
at: The grey part goes from sixty

slides.say: So it's a hundred ten minus sixty, fifty thousand.
Careful, a lot of students say a hundred ten, because that's where the grey part ends. But a part is the gap, from its bottom to its top.
Only the bottom part starts at zero. So we can read it straight from the axis.
Private cars in two thousand thirteen, the black part, go from zero to seventy. So seventy thousand.
The same data can be shown in many ways. One worker likes a table, another likes bars. The manager wants the total, so he gets a stack.
at: The same data can be shown

slides.say: One more kind, and it comes up quite often. Horizontal bars. They're ordinary bars, lying on their side.
This chart shows the average grades at the end of tenth grade, in two schools, Carob and Zucchini.
The example says, the average grade in English at Carob was seventy-five, and at Zucchini, eighty.
Now the values go across, on the bottom axis. The English bar at Carob reaches seventy-five. At Zucchini, it reaches eighty. It matches.
If it confuses you, turn the page in your mind. Then it's an ordinary bar chart.

slides: So in a bar chart, always ask two things. Is it stacked? Is one bar inside another? Then you won't read a hundred ten where the answer is fifty.
